question: to the Commission Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The recent outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus has exposed structural vulnerabilities in the EU’s biosecurity framework. The disease originated in areas where the EU acquis is suspended under Protocol No 10 on Cyprus annexed to the 2003 Act of Accession and subsequently spread to government-controlled areas, despite containment efforts. In the absence of a regulatory authority, the EU intervened through its Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community, providing vaccines and technical support. However, this raises concerns regarding the effectiveness of financial assistance without enforceable conditionality linked to EU veterinary standards. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risks posed to EU animal health and the internal market by the inability to ensure the application of EU sanitary standards in areas where the EU acquis is suspended?
Does the Commission intend to strengthen conditionality mechanisms linking EU financial assistance to compliance with EU veterinary and biosecurity protocols?
What additional measures might be envisaged to ensure coordinated and effective disease prevention and response across the entire territory of a Member State under such circumstances?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the author: Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Damian Boeselager (Verts/ALE). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) The EU legal framework governing animal health protection in the EU is in line with international standards and includes risk-based rules for imports of animals and products thereof into the EU. Relevant international standards have been incorporated into Council Regulation 866/20041 through Commission Decisions, that set out the terms under which goods can cross the line from the areas of the Republic of Cyprus (RoC) in which the RoC Government does not exercise effective control. Pursuant to Protocol No 10 of the 2003 Act of Accession2, the acquis is suspended in the mentioned areas. The Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community aims to improve the socio-economic situation of the Turkish Cypriot community and is implemented in line with EU policies. Regarding the foot-and-mouth disease in Cyprus, support provided through the Aid Programme has contributed to improving animal health in the northern part of the island in recent years. The Commission applies conditionalities adapted to the specific circumstances of the island and the size of the financial support available. It promotes a coordinated and effective disease prevention and response, including by supporting the work of the Veterinary Sub-Committee, under the Technical Committee for Health, established by the leaders of the two communities. An effective, all-island approach requires the engagement of both Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. The Commission reiterates that a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue, in line with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions, is the best path towards lasting and sustainable solutions to challenges affecting the entire island.
